catalog_quote: in Manange, polysyllabic words, a slightly heavier stress most often falls on the initial syllable of the root, regardless of the overall phonotactic structure of the phonological word. ... Perceptually speaking, Mananges speakers agree that the 'most accented' syllable is generally the first one. My own phonetic analyses confirm this, but overall there isn't a very noticeable difference in stress patterns on different syllables. Initial syllables typically show a somewhat longer vowel duration and a minimally higher amplitude of the vowel (by about 2 decibels) than do penultimate or final syllables. Of course, given that the tone system in this language is somewhat complicated, the same can be said for the stress system. I have noticed a number of words with phonetic evidence (through vowel duration and amplitude differences) of final stress. These words are listed below ... These word…
sweep_summary: Both sweep items are duplicate Glottolog records of one work, Hildebrandt 2005 (LTBA 28.1), which is already held (image-only scan + scanned) and was re-read: its suprasegmental section is entirely about word tone and it is silent on stress placement except one incidental 'unstressed (second) syllable' remark on p. 15, consistent with the catalog's root-initial coding. The catalog's deciding passage (Hildebrandt 2004, §2.6, pp. 37-39) was re-verified verbatim in the held text layer and stays the best first-hand statement; nothing read supersedes it. One new, weaker datum: the AUTOTYP Word Domains database (Bickel, Hildebrandt & Schiering; refetched from GitHub) codes Manange as 'Exactly 1 Main Stress, Penult' over 'stem ± prefix ± suffix ± particle' from 'Grammar Explicit' evidence, a label that diverges from 'root-initial' whenever a root is polysyllabic or prefixed; this is a secondary coding and merits a note, not a recoding. Unread candidates worth acquiring: Hildebrandt & Anderson 2023 'Word Prominence in Languages of Southern Asia' (OUP, high), Hildebrandt 2015 'The Prosodic Word' (OUP handbook, medium), Bickel, Hildebrandt & Schiering 2009 (De Gruyter, medium; source of the AUTOTYP coding), Hildebrandt 2013/2018 CUP sketch (low). Google Books API quota exhausted; sealang.net unreachable; DOI landing for the LTBA paper (dr.ntu.edu.sg) behind an AWS WAF captcha; OUP/Cambridge pages show no abstract.

new_statements.reading: An incidental, first-hand phonetic remark by the language's phonetician that the second syllable of a disyllable is the unstressed one (with vowel reduction there), which presupposes first-syllable prominence. The paper otherwise treats only tone (TBU = phonological word) and never addresses stress placement, so it is consistent with but far weaker than the catalog's deciding passage in Hildebrandt 2004 §2.6 (pp. 37-39: 'a slightly heavier stress most often falls on the initial syllable of the root, regardless of the overall phonotactic structure of the phonological word', with a lexical list of final-stress disyllables), which I re-read in the held text layer and which remains the best statement.

sources.note: An instrumental phonetics paper (Praat, four speakers) whose 'suprasegmental' section is entirely about the four-way word-tone system (TBU = phonological word; F0 trajectories, aspiration). Word stress is never treated; the only mention is the incidental parenthesis on p. 15 that a second syllable is 'unstressed', which presupposes first-syllable prominence in disyllables and is consistent with the 2004 grammar's root-initial stress. Vowel-duration data (pp. 21-25) are about open vs closed syllables and elicitation context, not stress position. scanned text grep for stress/accent/prominence/a…

sources.note: Database coding by Hildebrandt's own typology project: Manange has exactly one main lexical stress per phonological word, coded as PENULT, with the stress domain spanning stem plus prefix, suffix and particle. This differs in label from the 2004 grammar's 'initial syllable of the root, regardless of the overall phonotactic structure' (which places stress on the root even when a case enclitic or suffix follows, and lists lexical exceptions with final stress).
